content: Which prophet confronted David about his sin with Bathsheba?
explanation:
The correct answer is Nathan. In 2 Samuel 12:7, Nathan directly says to David: 'You are the man!'. He is the prophet who told the parable and confronted David about the Bathsheba incident.
- Gilead is incorrect because it is the name of a region (a land), not the name of a prophet.
- Ahijah was a prophet (1 Kings 11:29-30), but he lived and ministered later during the time of King Jeroboam, and was not the one who confronted David about this sin. This is a 'close' distractor because he was indeed a prophet, but from the wrong period and event.
- Jeremiah was a major prophet, but he lived and worked many centuries after David's time, so he could not have been the person in this event.
options: Gilead
Nathan
Ahijah
Jeremiah

content: How many years in total did David reign as king?
explanation: 2 Samuel 5:4-5 states: 'David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.' Therefore, David's total reign was 40 years. The correct answer is the valid combination of the numbers in the Scripture. The incorrect answers: (1) '42 years...' is close but incorrect in the detail of years in Jerusalem (35 instead of 33). (2) '33 years...' narrows the scope, taking only the years in Jerusalem while ignoring the time in Hebron. (3) '7 years...' is based on a common misunderstanding that David was only king in Hebron, not accounting for his entire reign.
options: 42 years (7 years in Hebron, 35 years in Jerusalem)
33 years (no specific breakdown)
7 years (only in Hebron, before moving to Jerusalem)
40 years (7 years in Hebron, 33 years in Jerusalem)

content: What did David do when the Ark of the Covenant was brought into Jerusalem?
explanation: The Scripture passage 2 Samuel 6:14-15 describes: 'David, wearing a linen ephod, danced before the LORD with all his might... So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet.' The correct answer is because the text directly says David 'danced with all his might.' Distractor 1 (Offering thanksgiving prayer) is close because David had a reverent attitude, but the specific action recorded is dancing, not praying at that moment. Distractor 2 (Standing still solemnly) is a common misunderstanding about worship posture, but the text describes energetic dancing. Distractor 3 (Offering a burnt sacrifice) is incorrect in detail; the offering of sacrifices (as in verse 13) occurred earlier on the journey, not as David's action right when the Ark was brought to Jerusalem as the question asks.
options: Danced before the Lord with all his might
Offering thanksgiving prayer before the Ark of the Covenant
Standing still solemnly and worshiping
Offering a burnt sacrifice immediately on the spot

content: What important promise did the Davidic Covenant (2 Samuel 7) contain?
explanation:
2 Samuel 7:12-13 records God's promise to David through the prophet Nathan: 'When your days are fulfilled, and you rest with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you... I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.' This is the crucial promise of an everlasting royal dynasty, fulfilled perfectly in the Messiah.

The correct answer is correct because it directly summarizes the promise of an everlasting throne for David's descendants.

Distractor 1 is wrong because that was David's initial intention (to build a temple for God, mentioned at the beginning of chapter 7), not God's promise to David.

Distractor 2 is wrong because the promise of a permanent land was central to the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15:18) and the people of Israel, not the main point of the Davidic covenant in this passage.

Distractor 3 (close but incorrect) is wrong because it errs on one key detail: the promise is 'forever' (everlasting), not limited only to 'the end of the period of the judges' (an earlier period in Israel's history).
options: David will have a sturdy cedar house built for him
David's descendants will be given a vast land forever
The throne of David's line will last until the end of the period of the judges
The throne of David's lineage would endure forever

content: To whom did David show kindness because of his promise to Jonathan?
explanation:
In 2 Samuel 9:1-7, David asks, 'Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?' (verse 1). Ziba the servant informs him that there is a son of Jonathan named Mephibosheth (verse 3). Therefore, the correct answer is 'Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan'.

- The distractor 'Bathsheba, daughter of Saul' (wrong_detail) is incorrect because Bathsheba is one of Saul's two daughters (2 Samuel 21:8), not the person David treated kindly in this passage.
- The distractor 'Ish-bosheth, son of Saul' (wrong_scope) is incorrect because Ish-bosheth is another son of Saul who had died before this event (2 Samuel 4), not the subject of the inquiry in 9:1-7.
- The distractor 'Shimei, of the house of Saul' (common_misconception) is incorrect because Shimei was from the tribe of Benjamin and the house of Saul (2 Samuel 16:5), but he is not mentioned in this passage and was not the one treated kindly for Jonathan's sake.
options: Bathsheba, daughter of Saul
Ish-bosheth, son of Saul
Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan
Shimei, of the house of Saul

content: When did David's great sin with Bathsheba begin?
explanation: Correct answer: 'When David stayed in Jerusalem instead of going to battle' (2 Samuel 11:1) – This is the initial context that led to all subsequent wrongful actions, when the king was not in his proper leadership position on the battlefield. Distractor 1 (close): 'When David sent someone to inquire about her' (v.3) – This action occurred immediately after, but the sin had already begun with the decision to stay. Distractor 2: 'When David sent someone to bring her to the palace' (v.4) – This is the next action, part of the sequence, not the starting point. Distractor 3: 'When David committed adultery with her' (v.4) – This is the climax of the sin, not when it began.
options: When David sent someone to inquire about her
When David sent someone to bring her to the palace
When David remained in Jerusalem instead of going to battle
When David committed adultery with her

content: What did David do to cover up his sin with Bathsheba?
explanation:
The Scripture passage 2 Samuel 11:14-17 clearly states: David wrote a letter to Joab, commanding him to 'set Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retreat from him, that he may be struck and die.' (verse 15). Therefore, the correct answer is that David arranged for Uriah to die in battle.

The incorrect answers: (1) 'Personally killing her husband Uriah at home' is close but incorrect in a key detail: David did not kill Uriah with his own hands but used a scheme in battle (11:15, 17). (2) 'Putting Uriah on a list of soldiers to be expelled' is incorrect in scope: this does not appear in the nearby passage; the passage only mentions Uriah being sent back to the battlefield with a secret letter (11:14). (3) 'Publicly confessing and asking for forgiveness' is a common misunderstanding based on a later event (2 Samuel 12, after Nathan's rebuke), but it was not the action David used to 'cover up' his sin in the immediate context of the question (11:14-17).
options: Personally killing her husband Uriah at home
Putting Uriah on a list of soldiers to be expelled
Arranged for her husband Uriah to die in battle
Publicly confessing and asking for forgiveness

content: When his son died, what did David say about his hope?
explanation: 2 Samuel 12:23 records David's words: 'I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.' This is the correct answer because David expresses his personal hope that he will meet his son again (after death), while acknowledging the reality that the child cannot come back to life. The incorrect options: 1) 'He will live again, but I will not meet him' is wrong because it misrepresents a key detail — in Scripture, David does not say the child will live again; 2) 'I will wait for him, and he will return to me' misses the point — while emotionally plausible, it is not what David actually said; 3) 'I cannot go to him anymore' misinterprets a nearby passage — this contradicts the mood of acceptance and hope expressed by David in the context.
options: I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me
He will live again, but I will not meet him
I will wait for him, and he will return to me
I cannot go to him anymore

content: Which of David's sons rebelled and proclaimed himself king?
explanation:
2 Samuel 15:13-14 records a messenger reporting to David: 'The hearts of the people of Israel are with Absalom.' and David said to his servants in Jerusalem: 'Arise, and let us flee; or else none of us will escape from Absalom. Make haste to depart, lest he overtake us quickly...' This passage describes the rebellion of Absalom, David's son, who declared himself king.
- The correct answer 'Absalom' is David's son who rebelled and declared himself king as described in 2 Samuel 15:13-14.
- Distractor 'Solomon' is incorrect because Solomon was David's son who succeeded to the throne legitimately, not through rebellion (this is a close distractor, only incorrect regarding the nature of the event).
- Distractor 'Amnon' is incorrect because Amnon was David's son who was killed by his half-brother Absalom in revenge for raping his sister, not someone who rebelled and declared himself king.
- Distractor 'Joab' is incorrect because Joab was the commander of David's army, not David's son, so he could not be the rebel in the context of the question.
options: Solomon
Amnon
Absalom
Joab

content: How did David react when Absalom died?
explanation: In 2 Samuel 18:33 (KJV), David wept bitterly and said, 'O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!' The correct answer accurately describes this reaction: weeping and wishing to die in his son's place. The incorrect answers: 1) 'Rejoicing...' is wrong because David was deeply grieved, not joyful; this is a common misunderstanding that the king would be pleased at the rebel's death. 2) 'Remaining silent...' is wrong because Scripture clearly records that David wept and cried out loudly. 3) 'Praying for God to have mercy...' is a plausible detail (showing compassion), but misses the key point: the text does not record this prayer but records David's wish to die instead; this distractor borrows from other grieving reactions in Scripture but is not the reaction recorded in this passage.
options: Rejoicing because the rebel had been punished
Remaining silent and showing no emotion
Praying for God to have mercy on his soul
Wept and wished he had died in his son's place

content: David's last words emphasized what about God's covenant?
explanation:
The Scripture passage 2 Samuel 23:5 quotes David: 'Is not my house right with God? Has he not made with me an everlasting covenant, arranged and secured in every part? Will he not bring to fruition my salvation...' This verse emphasizes the 'everlasting' and 'secure for all my house' nature of the covenant.

CORRECT ANSWER: 'An everlasting covenant, secure for all his house' — matches the content of verse 5, speaking of a permanent and safe covenant for all David's descendants.

INCORRECT DISTRACTORS:
1. 'A firm covenant, based on David's righteousness' (wrong_detail): While verses 3-4 mention the ruler's righteousness, the covenant emphasized here is based on God's promise, not on David's merit.
2. 'A covenant that applies only to David himself' (wrong_scope): Completely contrary to the 'for all his house' meaning in verse 5, this covenant extends to all his descendants.
3. 'A covenant guaranteeing immediate material prosperity for his descendants' (common_misconception): This is a common misinterpretation when explaining covenant promises; this passage emphasizes spiritual salvation and stability, not immediate material blessings.
options: An everlasting covenant, unchanging
A firm covenant, based on David's righteousness
A covenant that applies only to David himself
A covenant guaranteeing immediate material prosperity for his descendants

content: What did David say when buying the threshing floor to build an altar?
explanation:
In 2 Samuel 24:24, David replied to Araunah: 'I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing.' (NIV). This verse expresses the idea 'I do not want to offer a burnt offering to the LORD without paying the price.' THE CORRECT ANSWER is because it accurately reflects David's spirit of paying the full price.

DISTRACTOR 1 ('I will buy this threshing floor at a cheap price to offer to the LORD.') is WRONG because David did not bargain for a cheap price; he paid the full price (50 shekels of silver) and emphasized not taking something that cost him nothing (v. 24). This is a 'close but incorrect' distractor because it has the correct context of buying the threshing floor but is wrong on the key detail of the attitude of paying the full price.

DISTRACTOR 2 ('I want to offer a burnt offering to the LORD but do not want to pay the price.') is WRONG because it is completely opposite to David's spirit, who insisted on paying the price to make the offering meaningful. This is a common misunderstanding about the attitude of giving.

DISTRACTOR 3 ('I do not want to offer a burnt offering to the LORD without making a sacrifice.') is WRONG because the question asks about the reason when buying the threshing floor, which relates to paying the price, not the act of sacrifice itself. This answer is textually correct (it involves offering a burnt offering) but misses the focus of the question.
options: I will buy this threshing floor at a cheap price to offer to the LORD.
I want to offer a burnt offering to the LORD but do not want to pay the price.
I will not offer to the Lord sacrifices that cost me nothing
I do not want to offer a burnt offering to the LORD without making a sacrifice.

content: After hearing of Saul and Jonathan's death, what did David do?
explanation: The correct answer is 'Compose a lament for Saul and Jonathan,' because 2 Samuel 1:17 records: 'David took up this lament concerning Saul and his son Jonathan.' The incorrect answers: 1) 'Sing a hymn of thanksgiving' is wrong because the immediate context (1:18) only mentions David commanding that this lament be taught to the people of Judah; its content is mourning, not praise/thanksgiving. 2) 'Write a letter rebuking the people of Judah' is incorrect in detail, as in this passage David does not write any letter of rebuke. 3) 'Hold a funeral ceremony' is incorrect in scope; this is not mentioned in 1:17-27; David only mourns through the song, as the actual funeral had already been performed earlier by the people of Jabesh (1 Samuel 31:11-13).
options: Sing a hymn of thanksgiving to God
Composed a lament for Saul and Jonathan
Write a letter rebuking the people of Judah
Hold a funeral ceremony for Saul and Jonathan

content: Where was David anointed king over the house of Judah?
explanation:
The correct answer is 'Hebron' because 2 Samuel 2:4 clearly states: 'Then the men of Judah came to Hebron and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah.'

The incorrect answers:
- 'Bethlehem' is incorrect because this is David's hometown (1 Samuel 17:12), but it is not where he was anointed king of Judah; this is a mistake of confusing it with a nearby detail.
- 'Jerusalem' is incorrect because this is the city David later captured and made the capital of all Israel (2 Samuel 5:6-7), not the initial place where he was anointed king of Judah; this is a common misunderstanding.
- 'Jericho' is incorrect because this is another famous city, unrelated to this anointing event; this is an error of detail (name).
options: Hebron
Bethlehem
Jerusalem
Jericho

content: What stronghold did David capture to make his capital?
explanation:
2 Samuel 5:7 records: 'Nevertheless, David captured the stronghold of Zion; that is, the city of David.' This is the place David chose as his capital, later known as Jerusalem. The correct answer is 'the stronghold of Zion (Jerusalem)' because the Bible clearly records this event.

Incorrect answers:
- 'Gibeath (Saul's hometown)': Incorrect detail. Gibeath was Saul's city (1 Samuel 10:26), not the place David captured as his capital. This is a plausible distractor as it is an important city from this period, but it involves the wrong person and key event.
- 'Jericho (the first city conquered)': Biblically accurate but irrelevant to the question. Jericho was conquered under Joshua (Joshua 6) and is unrelated to David establishing his capital.
- 'Rabbah (the capital of Ammon)': Incorrect scope. Rabbah was the capital of the Ammonites, conquered by David later (2 Samuel 12:26-31), not the place he initially chose as his capital.
options: Gibeath (Saul's hometown)
Jericho (the first city conquered)
Rabbah (the capital of Ammon)
The stronghold of Zion (Jerusalem)

content: Who died for putting his hand on the Ark when bringing it to Jerusalem?
explanation: The correct answer is Uzzah. According to 2 Samuel 6:6-7, Uzzah reached out to steady the Ark of the Covenant when the oxen stumbled, and God's anger burned against Uzzah, striking him dead there. Distractor 'Ahio' is incorrect because Ahio was walking in front of the Ark (verse 4), not the one who died. Distractor 'David' is incorrect because David was the king overseeing the transportation of the Ark (verse 5), not the one who died in this incident. Distractor 'Solomon' is incorrect because Solomon was David's son, appears after this event, and is not related to the story of moving the Ark in 2 Samuel 6.
options: Ahio
Uzzah
David
Solomon

content: The tragedy in David's family in 2 Samuel 13 involves whom?
explanation: The question asks about the tragedy in David's family specifically described in 2 Samuel 13. The correct answer is 'Amnon and Tamar' because the entire chapter 13 focuses on Amnon's rape of his half-sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13:1-22). The distractor 'Absalom and Amnon' is close because Absalom was Tamar's full brother and later killed Amnon in revenge, but the central pair in the tragedy is Amnon and Tamar. The distractor 'David and Bathsheba' is out of scope because that story occurs in chapter 11 and is a different tragedy. The distractor 'Jonathan and Tamar' is a common misunderstanding, as Jonathan was David's friend and is not involved in the tragedy of chapter 13.
options: Absalom and Amnon
David and Bathsheba
Jonathan and Tamar
Amnon and Tamar

content: Whom did Joab use to persuade David to bring Absalom back?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER: 'A wise woman from Tekoa' (2 Samuel 14:2). Joab sent a wise woman from Tekoa to King David, instructing her to tell a parable so the king would agree to let Absalom return.

INCORRECT DISTRACTOR 1 ('A wise woman from Bethlehem'): Incorrect location detail. Bethlehem was David's hometown (1 Samuel 16:1), but this woman was from Tekoa (2 Samuel 14:2).

INCORRECT DISTRACTOR 2 ('A wise woman who was a relative of Joab'): Incorrect scope. The Scripture never mentions any family relationship between this woman and Joab; she was only enlisted by Joab to help (2 Samuel 14:1-2).

INCORRECT DISTRACTOR 3 ('A wise woman hired by Joab for money'): Common misunderstanding of motive. The Scripture does not say Joab paid her money; he only 'sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman' and 'instructed her what to say' (2 Samuel 14:2-3).
options: A wise woman of Tekoa
A wise woman from Bethlehem
A wise woman who was a relative of Joab
A wise woman hired by Joab for money

content: When David fled from Absalom, who followed him along the way and cursed him?
explanation: The correct answer is Shimei, son of Gera, based on 2 Samuel 16:5-13, which describes Shimei cursing and throwing stones at David as he fled. Absalom was the enemy David was fleeing from, but he was not the one cursing him (common mistake). Joab was a loyal general of David and did not curse him in this passage (out of scope). Ahithophel was Absalom's counselor and appears in the same story but was not the one cursing (nearby passage confusion).
options: Absalom, son of David
Shimei son of Gera
Joab, son of Zeruiah
Ahithophel, the Gilonite

content: In the song of thanksgiving in 2 Samuel 22, what does David call the LORD?
explanation:
The question specifically asks about the titles David calls the LORD in 2 Samuel 22:2-3. The Scripture records: 'The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer; my God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold.' Therefore, the correct answer is 'The rock, the fortress, the deliverer, the shield, the high tower' (with 'high tower' corresponding to 'my stronghold').

The incorrect answers: (1) '... and the Shepherd' is an incorrect detail, as the title 'Shepherd' does not appear in this passage (though it is common in other Psalms). (2) '... and the Almighty' mistakes a nearby passage, as the title 'the Almighty' (El Shaddai) is not found in 2 Samuel 22:2-3. (3) 'The Redeemer, the Protector, and the Guide,' while possibly theologically accurate in meaning, misses the point of the question because they are not the titles listed in this specific passage.
options: The rock, the fortress, the deliverer, the shield, the high tower, and the Shepherd
The rock, the fortress, the deliverer, and the Almighty
Rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, stronghold
The Redeemer, the Protector, and the Guide

content: What outward signs did the messenger who brought news of Saul's death display when he arrived at the camp?
options: Torn clothes and dust on his head
Holding the king's broken sword in his hand
Dressed in black mourning garments from head to toe
Wearing the king's crown and draped in the king's robe
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 1:2) records that the man from Saul's camp came with 'his clothes torn and dirt on his head' as a sign of mourning. (B) 'the king's broken sword' is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail). (C) 'black mourning garments' confuses this with another custom; the text only mentions torn clothes (common_misconception). (D) 'wearing the crown and draped in the king's robe' describes what the man brought to David, not the outward signs he himself displayed (wrong_detail).

content: What people group did the messenger claim to belong to when recounting Saul's death?
options: The Amalekites
The Philistines
The Gibeonites
The Moabites
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 1:8) records that when Saul asked 'Who are you?', the man replied 'I am an Amalekite.' (B) The Philistines were the enemy fighting against Saul at Mount Gilboa, not the messenger (near_passage). (C) The Gibeonites relate to a later period and are not present in this passage (wrong_scope). (D) Moab was where David once sent his parents for safekeeping; this man was not Moabite (wrong_detail).

content: Why did David order the execution of the messenger who claimed to have killed Saul?
options: Because he claimed to have killed the one anointed by the LORD
Because he lied that Jonathan had survived
Because he stole the king's crown and gold armlet
Because he fled from the battle against the Philistines
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 1:16) records David's charge: 'Your blood be on your head, for your own mouth has testified against you, saying, "I have killed the LORD's anointed."' The core offense was striking the LORD's anointed. (B) This misrepresents the text: the messenger reported that Jonathan had died, not that he was still alive (wrong_detail). (C) Though the man did bring the crown and armlet, that was not the stated reason for his execution — it was his claim of having killed the king (true_but_off). (D) Fleeing the battlefield was not the charge David brought against him (wrong_detail).

content: What is the name of the lament David composed to mourn Saul and Jonathan?
options: The Song of the Bow
The Songs of Ascents
The Song of Gilboa
The Song of the Anointed One
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 1:18) records that David taught 'the people of Judah the Song of the Bow' (the lament of the bow). (B) 'The Songs of Ascents' refers to Psalms 120–134 from a later era, which falls outside the scope of this passage (wrong_scope). (C) 'Gilboa' is indeed the location of the battle and is mentioned within the lament, but it is not the title of the song (true_but_off). (D) 'The Anointed One' is a phrase connected to the reason for executing the Amalekite, not the name of the lament (near_passage).

content: Who installed Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, as king over Israel?
options: Abner, commander of Saul's army
Joab, commander of David's army
Samuel, the prophet
Ahimelech, the priest
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 2:8–9) states that 'Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth... and made him king' over Israel. (B) Joab was the commander on David's side, belonging to the opposing faction (near_passage). (C) Samuel had already died before this event and could not have installed a king at this point (wrong_scope). (D) Ahimelech was a priest from an earlier period and played no role in making Ish-bosheth king (wrong_detail).

content: Where did the first clash between Abner's forces and Joab's forces break out?
options: By the pool of Gibeon
By the well of Bethlehem
On the plain of Gilboa
At the ford of the Jordan
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 2:13) states that both sides 'met together at the pool of Gibeon,' sitting opposite each other on either side of the pool before engaging in battle. (B) 'the well of Bethlehem' is associated with the story of the three mighty men risking their lives to draw water in a later chapter — a different passage (near_passage). (C) Gilboa is where Saul fell in chapter 1, not the location of this encounter (near_passage). (D) 'the ford of the Jordan' is where Abner retreated after the battle, not the site of the first clash (wrong_detail).

content: Asahel pursued Abner and was killed; which option correctly describes the sequence of events leading to his death?
options: Abner warned him repeatedly to turn back, but Asahel refused, so Abner thrust the butt of his spear through his stomach
Abner ambushed him in a forest and suddenly struck Asahel from behind with a sword
Asahel was hit by an arrow shot by Abner's soldiers during the pursuit
Joab accidentally shot Asahel while aiming at Abner who was fleeing in front of him
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 2:21-23) Abner twice urged Asahel to 'turn aside' and stop pursuing him, but Asahel refused; finally Abner 'struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, so that the spear came out at his back' (correct — requires careful reading of the sequence). (B) wrong weapon and manner: it was the butt of a spear thrust as Asahel kept pressing forward, not a sword strike from behind in a forest ambush (wrong_detail). (C) 'hit by an arrow' is not in the text — Asahel died from the spear butt (wrong_detail). (D) Joab was Asahel's brother and arrived later; he was not the one who caused the death — this wrongly attributes the act to Joab (common_misconception).

content: The sons of David listed in this chapter were all born in which city?
options: In Hebron
In Jerusalem
In Bethlehem
In Shiloh
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 3:2) 'And sons were born to David at Hebron.' (B) Jerusalem only became the capital in a later chapter; these sons were born before that (wrong_scope). (C) Bethlehem was David's hometown, not the birthplace of these sons (common_misconception). (D) Shiloh was where the tabernacle was kept during the time of the judges and is unrelated here (wrong_detail).

content: What accusation by Ish-bosheth enraged Abner and caused him to decide to switch his allegiance to David?
options: Accusing Abner of sleeping with Rizpah, Saul's concubine
Accusing Abner of embezzling spoils of war after the battle of Gibeon
Accusing Abner of plotting to assassinate Ish-bosheth himself
Accusing Abner of letting Asahel escape from the battle
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 3:7-8) Ish-bosheth rebuked Abner, 'Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?' (Rizpah), causing Abner to become furious and swear to transfer the kingdom to David. (B) 'embezzling spoils of war' does not appear in the text (wrong_detail). (C) 'plotting to assassinate Ish-bosheth' reverses the storyline — Ish-bosheth was later killed by others, and this was never the accusation leveled here (common_misconception). (D) Asahel never escaped — he was killed by Abner in chapter 2, making this accusation impossible (near_passage).

content: Joab killed Abner at the gate of Hebron; what was Joab's primary motive for acting?
options: To avenge Asahel, his brother, whom Abner had killed at Gibeon
To carry out a secret order from David who wanted to eliminate Abner
To prevent Abner from revealing military plans to Ish-bosheth
To compete for the position of commander that David had promised to give Abner
explanation: ESV (2 Samuel 3:27, 30) Joab stabbed Abner 'to avenge the blood of Asahel his brother' — the text explicitly states the motive was blood vengeance because Asahel was killed at Gibeon. (B) wrong: David publicly declared his innocence, mourned Abner, and cursed the house of Joab — he gave no secret order (common_misconception). (C) 'preventing Abner from revealing plans' sounds plausible but is not the reason the text gives; Abner was already on David's side (true_but_off). (D) 'competing for the position of commander' is a reasonable inference, but the text attributes the motive to blood vengeance, not rivalry over rank (true_but_off).

content: What was the name of Jonathan's son who was lame in both feet because he fell as a child?
options: Mephibosheth
Ish-bosheth
Rechab
Baanah
explanation: 2 Samuel 4:4 records that Jonathan had a son who was lame in both feet, named Mephibosheth, who was dropped by his nurse as she fled. 'Ish-bosheth' was Saul's son who was reigning as king and was killed in this chapter — he was not Jonathan's son (wrong_detail). 'Rechab' and 'Baanah' were the two men who murdered Ish-bosheth (wrong_detail).

content: Under what circumstances did Rechab and Baanah kill Ish-bosheth?
options: While he was taking a midday nap on his bed
While he was feasting with his officials
While he was going out to battle against the Philistines
While he was offering sacrifices at the temple
explanation: 2 Samuel 4:5–7 records that the two men entered the house during the heat of the day while Ish-bosheth was lying down for his midday rest, then stabbed him and cut off his head. He was not at a feast (wrong_detail), not going out to battle (wrong_scope), and not offering sacrifices (wrong_scope).

content: When Rechab and Baanah brought the head of Ish-bosheth to present to David, how did David respond to them?
options: He commanded that the two men be killed and their bodies hung beside the pool at Hebron
He rewarded them and appointed them as commanders in his army
He spared their lives but banished them from the land permanently
He had them imprisoned to await trial at a later time
explanation: 2 Samuel 4:12 records that David commanded his servants to kill the two men, cut off their hands and feet, and hang their bodies by the pool at Hebron, for he regarded killing a righteous man as he lay on his bed as a wicked crime. Rewarding them is entirely contrary to David's actual response (common_misconception). Sparing and banishing them (wrong_detail) and imprisoning them to await trial (wrong_detail) both contradict the text, which states David had them executed immediately.

content: Who came to Hebron to make a covenant and anoint David as king over all Israel?
options: All the tribes of Israel
The tribe of Judah alone
The priests at Shiloh
The commanders of Saul's army
explanation: 2 Samuel 5:1–3 records that all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron, made a covenant with him, and anointed him king. The tribe of Judah had already anointed David at an earlier time (2 Sam 2:4), so that answer only applies to a prior episode (near_passage). The priests at Shiloh (wrong_scope) and Saul's commanders (wrong_detail) were not the parties who came to make this covenant.

content: What did the Jebusites mock David about when he led his forces to attack their city?
options: Even the blind and the lame would be enough to keep him from entering the city
His army was too small compared to the forces inside the city
God had abandoned him just as He had abandoned Saul
Their city walls had never been breached by anyone before
explanation: 2 Samuel 5:6 records that the Jebusites said David could not come in here, for even the blind and the lame would repel him — a taunt meant to belittle David's military confidence. Mocking the size of his army (wrong_detail), claiming God had abandoned him as He had abandoned Saul (common_misconception), and boasting that the walls were impregnable (true_but_off — the city was indeed well-fortified, but that is not the taunt the text records) are all absent from the recorded mockery.

content: Which king sent messengers along with cedar wood and craftsmen to build a palace for David?
options: Hiram, king of Tyre
Abimelech, king of Gerar
Hadadezer, king of Zobah
Toi, king of Hamath
explanation: 2 Samuel 5:11 records that Hiram, king of Tyre, sent messengers to David along with cedar wood, carpenters, and stonemasons to build a house for David. Hadadezer king of Zobah was the one David defeated later (near_passage, 2 Sam 8). Toi king of Hamath sent his son to congratulate David after that victory (near_passage, 2 Sam 8). Abimelech king of Gerar belongs to the time of Abraham (wrong_scope).

content: In the two occasions when the Philistines came up to fight in the Valley of Rephaim, how did the LORD instruct David to fight differently each time?
options: The first time he charged directly at the enemy; the second time he circled around to ambush from behind the balsam trees
The first time he circled around to ambush; the second time he charged directly at the enemy
Both times he had to wait until he heard the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees before attacking
Both times he launched a direct frontal assault on the enemy camp
explanation: Both battles in 2 Samuel 5 must be compared: in the first battle (vv. 19–20), the LORD told David to go up, and he attacked and broke through the enemy at Baal-perazim. In the second battle (vv. 23–24), the LORD told him not to go up directly but to circle around behind them and wait until he heard the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees before striking. Reversing the order of the two battles is almost-right (wrong_detail). Saying both times required waiting for the sound in the balsam trees confuses the sign unique to the second battle with the first (almost-right, wrong_detail). Saying both times involved a direct charge omits the ambush tactic of the second battle (wrong_scope).

content: Why did Michal, the daughter of Saul, despise David in her heart when she looked through the window?
options: Because she saw the king leaping and dancing before the LORD with all his might
Because she saw the king offering too many costly sacrifices
Because she saw the king letting the people carry the ark instead of carrying it himself
Because she saw that the king had forgotten to invite her to the procession of the ark
explanation: 2 Samuel 6:16 records that when the ark entered the city, Michal looked through the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart. Criticizing the cost of the sacrifices (wrong_detail) and the manner of carrying the ark (near_passage — v. 13 mentions those carrying the ark pausing to sacrifice after every six steps, which is unrelated to the cause of her contempt) are both wrong. The claim that she was forgotten and not invited (common_misconception) does not appear in the text.

content: After the incident at the threshing floor, at whose house did David leave the ark of the LORD for three months?
options: Obed-edom the Gittite
Uzzah, son of Abinadab
Ahio, son of Abinadab
Nathan the prophet
explanation: 2 Samuel 6:10–11 records that David brought the ark to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it remained for three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and his entire household. Uzzah is the man who died when he reached out his hand to steady the ark (near_passage). Ahio is the one who walked before the ark as it was being transported (near_passage). Nathan the prophet does not appear until chapter 7 (wrong_scope).

content: When Michal rebuked David's conduct on the day the ark was brought in, what attitude did the king's reply reveal, and what was the outcome for her life?
options: The king was willing to humble himself even more before the LORD, and Michal had no child to the day of her death
The king admitted his fault and asked forgiveness, and Michal was restored to honor
The king angrily sent her back to her father's house, and Michal remarried another man
The king left in silence without answering, and Michal was confined in the palace until her death
explanation: Both David's reply and the outcome must be analyzed: 2 Samuel 6:21–22 records that David answered that he was dancing before the LORD and would humble himself even more, regarding himself as lowly while the servant girls would hold him in honor; v. 23 records that Michal had no child to the day of her death. The option 'admitted his fault and was restored' directly contradicts David's defiant response and the outcome of childlessness (common_misconception). 'Sent her back to her father's house and she remarried' conflates events involving Palti from an earlier period (near_passage, 1 Sam 25 / 2 Sam 3) — almost-right but wrong on the outcome. 'Left in silence, she was confined until death' invents an attitude and a punishment not found in the text (wrong_detail).

content: What disproportion troubled David when he confided in the prophet Nathan?
options: The king lived in a house of cedar while the Ark of the Covenant was under a tent
The king was wealthy while the people were starving throughout the land
The king was at rest while his soldiers still had to go to war
The king had many wives while the officials had no families
explanation: 2 Sam 7:2 records David saying: 'See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent.' Answer A is correct. B is wrong because the rich-poor comparison is not in the text (wrong_detail). C is wrong because the rest was something God had granted (7:1), not what troubled the king (wrong_scope). D mentions wives and officials, which is unrelated to this passage (wrong_scope).

content: According to the word of the LORD through Nathan, who would be the one to build a temple for His name?
options: David's son
David himself after he had achieved victory
The prophet Nathan on the king's behalf
The high priest Abiathar
explanation: 2 Sam 7:12-13 records God's promise to raise up David's offspring after him: 'He shall build a house for my name.' Answer A (David's son, namely Solomon) is correct. B is wrong because God clearly said David would NOT build it (7:5, wrong_detail). C is wrong because Nathan was only the messenger, not the builder (wrong_scope). D names a priest who was never given this task (wrong_scope).

content: Among David's military campaigns in chapter 8, which nation did he defeat and require to pay tribute by being measured with a line?
options: The Moabites
The Philistines
The Amalekites
The Ammonites
explanation: 2 Sam 8:2 records that David defeated Moab and 'he measured them with a line, making them lie down on the ground,' determining who would live and die, and the Moabites became subject to him and brought tribute. Answer A is correct. B (Philistines) were defeated in 8:1 but the text contains no detail about measuring with a line (near_passage). C (Amalekites) do not appear in chapter 8 (wrong_scope). D (Ammonites) is the campaign of the following chapter, not this one (wrong_scope).

content: What was the name of Jonathan's son, crippled in both feet, whom David sought out in order to show kindness?
options: Mephibosheth
Ziba
Micah
Ish-bosheth
explanation: 2 Sam 9:6 records that Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, came to David; verse 3 states that he was 'crippled in his feet.' Answer A is correct. B (Ziba) was a former servant of Saul's household, not Jonathan's son (wrong_detail). C (Micah) was Mephibosheth's own son (9:12), not the one David was seeking (near_passage). D (Ish-bosheth) was Saul's son who had already died, not Jonathan's son (wrong_scope).

content: After hearing God's promise, how did David respond in a way that demonstrated humility?
options: He went in and sat before the LORD and confessed that he and his house were unworthy
He immediately ordered materials to be prepared to begin building the temple
He offered burnt offerings and danced before the Ark of the Covenant
He summoned the elders to announce the promise to all the people
explanation: 2 Sam 7:18 records that King David 'went in and sat before the LORD' and said: 'Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?' — expressing his sense of complete unworthiness. Answer A is correct. B is wrong because God had already said David's son would build the temple, so David would not have started construction (wrong_detail, almost-right because it connects to the temple theme). C confuses the scene of dancing when the Ark was brought up in chapter 6, not here (near_passage). D mentions announcing the promise to all the people, which has no place in this private prayer passage (wrong_scope).

content: Why did David continually triumph in all the campaigns described in chapter 8?
options: Because the LORD gave him victory wherever he went
Because he had the most powerful army in the region
Because the neighboring nations had been weakened after years of civil war
Because he formed a military alliance with King Hiram of Tyre
explanation: 2 Sam 8:6 and 8:14 both record the same explanation: 'the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.' Answer A is correct — the cause is God's gift. B credits military strength, contrary to the theological emphasis of the text (common_misconception). C infers about the condition of the surrounding nations, which is not found in the text (wrong_detail, almost-right because it sounds plausible). D confuses this with King Hiram sending cedar wood to build the palace in chapter 5, not the cause of the military victories in chapter 8 (near_passage).

content: What specific acts of kindness did David show to Mephibosheth?
options: He restored all the land of Saul and had Mephibosheth eat at the king's table always
He appointed him as a military commander and gave him his own army
He gave him rule over part of the land of Moab that had just been conquered
He gave him a royal daughter in marriage and made him the king's son-in-law
explanation: 2 Sam 9:7 records David saying, 'I will restore to you all the land of Saul your grandfather, and you shall eat at my table always.' Answer A is correct. B is wrong because Mephibosheth was crippled in both feet and was not appointed as a military commander (wrong_detail). C mixes in the land of Moab from chapter 8 into the context of chapter 9, which is incorrect (near_passage). D refers to giving a daughter in marriage and making a son-in-law, which belongs to the earlier story of Michal and David with Saul, not this passage (wrong_scope, almost-right because it is also a form of royal favor).

content: When God said of David's son, 'If he commits iniquity, I will discipline him… but my steadfast love will not depart from him,' what characteristic of the covenant does this reveal?
options: The covenant endures even with discipline; steadfast love is not withdrawn as it was from Saul
The covenant is entirely unconditional, so David's son will never be disciplined
The covenant is only valid as long as David's son keeps the law fully
The covenant will transfer to another lineage if David's son commits a serious sin
explanation: 2 Sam 7:14-15 records: 'If he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men… but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul.' The text places discipline IN PARALLEL with enduring steadfast love, and directly contrasts this with Saul — so A is correct (requires comparison, Bloom Analyze). B is wrong because it denies the very clause 'if he commits iniquity, I will discipline him' (wrong_detail, almost-right because the covenant is indeed enduring). C is wrong because it makes the covenant conditional, contradicting 'my steadfast love will not depart from him' (common_misconception, almost-right because it sounds like conditional covenant theology). D is wrong because the promise is that David's house and throne 'shall be established forever' (7:16), not transferred to another line (wrong_scope).

content: Compared to how kings of that era typically treated survivors of a previous dynasty, in what way did David's action toward the house of Saul in chapter 9 stand out?
options: He actively sought out survivors to show kindness for the sake of his covenant with Jonathan
He spared the survivors but required them to leave the land of Judah entirely
He kept the survivors close as hostages to prevent the house of Saul from rebelling
He showed kindness to the survivors but confiscated all their land for the royal treasury
explanation: 2 Sam 9:1 records David asking, 'Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?' Unlike the common practice of eliminating a previous royal bloodline, David ACTIVELY sought out survivors to show them kindness — this requires comparing motivation with historical context (Bloom Analyze), so A is correct. B is wrong because David had Mephibosheth live in Jerusalem and eat at the king's table, not sent away (wrong_detail, almost-right). C is wrong because eating at the king's table was an honor, not captivity as a hostage (common_misconception, almost-right because it sounds like political strategy). D is wrong because 9:7 records David RESTORING the land of Saul to Mephibosheth, not confiscating it (wrong_detail).

content: According to the summary at the end of chapter 8, how did David rule over all the people of Israel?
options: He administered justice and equity to all his people
He ruled with absolute power and imposed heavy taxes
He delegated all judicial matters to the Levitical priests
He expanded his territory but neglected internal governance of the land
explanation: 2 Sam 8:15 records: 'David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people.' Answer A is correct. B contradicts the description of 'justice and equity,' and heavy taxation is not mentioned in the text (wrong_detail). C is wrong because David himself ruled and adjudicated; although the list of officials in 8:16-18 mentions priests, they did not hold all judicial authority (near_passage, almost-right because the following verses do list religious offices). D contradicts the text's emphasis that David ruled his people with justice and equity, with no suggestion of neglecting internal governance (wrong_scope).

content: Why did David want to show kindness to Hanun?
options: Because Hanun's father Nahash had previously shown kindness to David
Because Hanun was David's relative on his mother's side
Because David wanted to form a military alliance against the Philistines
Because God commanded David to help the Ammonites
explanation: David said, 'I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father dealt loyally with me' (2 Samuel 10:2). The option about a maternal relative is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail). A military alliance against the Philistines is a motive not mentioned — it misattributes David's purpose (wrong_detail). God commanding David is incorrect; this was David's personal initiative, not a divine command (wrong_detail).

content: How did Hanun humiliate David's messengers?
options: He shaved off half their beards and cut their garments in half, to their hips
He had them chained and thrown into a dark dungeon for many days
He stripped them of all their clothing and drove them out of the city
He beat them and forced them to bow before the gods of the Ammonites
explanation: Hanun 'took David's servants and shaved off half the beard of each and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips' (2 Samuel 10:4). Throwing them into a dungeon is a different action not found in the text (wrong_detail). Stripping all their clothing is an exaggerated distortion — the text only says half their garments were cut (wrong_detail). Forcing them to bow before Ammonite gods is a fabricated detail with no basis in the text (wrong_detail).

content: Whom did David send carrying the letter ordering that Uriah be placed in the most dangerous position in battle so that he would be killed?
options: Uriah the Hittite himself — the very man condemned to die
A personal trusted messenger of David
Absalom, David's son
Abishai, the brother of the commander Joab
explanation: David 'wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah' (2 Samuel 11:14), meaning Uriah himself carried the letter that sealed his own death. A personal trusted messenger is a plausible but textually incorrect detail (wrong_detail). Absalom had no involvement in this event whatsoever (wrong_scope). Abishai was a real figure in the battle but was not the one who carried the letter (wrong_detail).

content: In the parable Nathan told David, what did the rich man take from the poor man to serve his guest?
options: The poor man's one little ewe lamb that he had raised like a daughter
The fattest ox from the poor man's herd
The vineyard the poor man had carefully tended
The silver the poor man had saved up over a long time
explanation: The rich man 'took the poor man's lamb' — which the poor man had raised 'like a daughter' (2 Samuel 12:3–4). The fattest ox is a different animal, not the one in the parable (wrong_detail). The vineyard recalls the story of Naboth in another book, making it the wrong passage (wrong_scope). Silver saved up is a fabricated detail; the parable is about the lamb (wrong_detail).

content: After humiliating David's messengers, what did the Ammonites realize that led them to hire foreign troops for reinforcement?
options: They realized they had made themselves odious to David
They realized their army was far too small compared to Israel
They realized the LORD was with David
They realized their cities were not fortified enough to withstand attack
explanation: 'When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David,' they sent and hired the Syrians (2 Samuel 10:6). Their motivation was the awareness that they had gravely offended David. Having too small an army is a reasonable inference but is not what the text states (wrong_detail). Acknowledging that the LORD was with David is something the pagan Ammonites never confessed — this misattributes a spiritual motive to them (common_misconception). Insufficiently fortified cities is a fabricated detail unrelated to their decision to hire troops (wrong_detail).

content: When Joab arrayed his forces between the Syrians and the Ammonites, with what spirit did he encourage his soldiers?
options: Be of good courage for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him
Fight with all your might for the glory of King David who now reigns over us
Be fully assured that the LORD has promised them complete and total victory
Withdraw in good order if the Syrians prove too strong to withstand
explanation: Joab said: 'Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him' (2 Samuel 10:12 ESV). Fighting for King David's glory is a wrong emphasis — Joab focused on the people and the cities of God, not royal prestige (wrong_detail). A promise of complete and certain victory is not mentioned; Joab committed the outcome to God's will rather than declaring guaranteed success (wrong_detail). Withdrawing directly contradicts the call to 'be of good courage and fight courageously' (wrong_detail).

content: Why did Uriah refuse to go home and sleep with his wife even though David tried to arrange the opportunity for him?
options: Because the ark of the covenant and the army were in the open field, he could not bring himself to enjoy ease and comfort
Because he had discovered David's sin with Bathsheba and was deliberately avoiding the situation
Because military law absolutely prohibited soldiers from being with their wives during wartime
Because he was angry with Bathsheba and no longer wished to live with her
explanation: Uriah said: 'The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife?' (2 Samuel 11:11 ESV). His loyalty to his comrades was the reason he refused. That Uriah knew of David's sin is a false inference; the text gives no indication he was aware of it (common_misconception). An absolute prohibition by military law is a false attribution; this was a personal choice of honor, not a legal requirement (wrong_detail). Anger at Bathsheba is pure fabrication with no basis in the text (wrong_detail).

content: In the judgment pronounced through Nathan, what consequences did God foretell would come upon David's house because of his sin?
options: The sword would never depart from his house, and evil would rise up against him from within his own household
His kingdom would be immediately taken from his hands and given to another
He would be struck with leprosy and would have to live in isolation until his death
The entire city of Jerusalem would be besieged and destroyed by his enemies
explanation: The LORD declared: 'The sword shall never depart from your house... I will raise up evil against you out of your own house' (2 Samuel 12:10–11 ESV). That the kingdom would be immediately stripped away is wrong; David's throne was not removed as Saul's had been (wrong_detail). Leprosy was a punishment that fell on a different king (Uzziah); this is the wrong passage's scope (wrong_scope). Jerusalem being besieged and destroyed is not part of this pronouncement; the calamity would arise from within David's own household (wrong_detail).

content: David's behavior after the child died — rising, washing, worshiping, then eating — astonished his servants; what view of life and death does this conduct reveal?
options: Fasting and pleading had meaning only while the child lived; now that the child was dead, he would go to the child, though the child could not return to him
Prolonged mourning was entirely futile because all things had been predetermined and could never be changed
He had been told by the prophet Nathan that God would raise the child to life, so there was no longer any reason to grieve
He believed that a proper, solemn funeral was more important than continued fasting, so he turned to making burial arrangements
explanation: David explained: 'While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, "Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?" But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me' (2 Samuel 12:21–23 ESV). The reasoning that 'all things are predetermined, so mourning is futile' imposes a fatalistic philosophy on the text — David did pray while the child lived precisely because he believed God could show mercy (common_misconception). Nathan foretelling that the child would be raised to life is pure fabrication; Nathan had clearly stated the child would die (wrong_detail). Shifting focus to arranging a solemn funeral falsely attributes David's motive; he was emphasizing the irreversibility of death, not turning to funeral logistics (wrong_detail).
tags: David and the Death of His Child

content: When David confessed, 'I have sinned against the LORD,' Nathan replied that the king's sin had been forgiven; what distinction did Nathan draw between David being forgiven and the consequences he must still bear?
options: David would not die for his sin, but the child just born would die because David had given the LORD's enemies occasion to blaspheme
David had been completely forgiven, so both he and the newborn child would be safe
David must personally offer the prescribed sin offering before his forgiveness could be considered fully complete
David would have to die for his sin, but in recompense the child would live and one day succeed him on the throne
explanation: Nathan declared: 'The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child who is born to you shall die' (2 Samuel 12:13–14 ESV). That both would be safe directly contradicts the explicit announcement that the child would die (wrong_detail). That a sin offering was required before forgiveness took effect is a false attribution; Nathan proclaimed the sin forgiven immediately, without any sacrificial condition (common_misconception). That David would die while the child would live is a complete reversal of Nathan's words; it is the king who would live and the child who would die (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Samuel 13, which of David's sons fell deeply in love with his half-sister Tamar?
options: Absalom
Adonijah
Amnon
Solomon
explanation: 2 Samuel 13:1 records that Amnon, David's son, loved Tamar, the beautiful sister of Absalom. 'Absalom' was Tamar's full brother, who later avenged her — he is not the one who loved her (wrong_scope). 'Adonijah' was another of David's sons but rose to prominence in 1 Kings, outside this story (wrong_scope). 'Solomon' was the son of Bathsheba who succeeded David and had no connection to this event (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Samuel 13, on what occasion did Absalom order his servants to kill Amnon?
options: At Absalom's sheep-shearing festival
At the wedding feast of one of David's sons
At a sacrifice ceremony in Hebron
On the day of the new moon at the royal palace
explanation: 2 Samuel 13:23-29 records that Absalom invited all the king's sons to his sheep-shearing at Baal-hazor, then commanded his servants to kill Amnon there. 'A wedding feast' does not appear in this passage (wrong_detail). 'A sacrifice at Hebron' was the pretext Absalom used later when he rebelled in chapter 15, not the occasion of Amnon's murder (near_passage). 'The day of the new moon at the royal palace' is the context for David's absence in 1 Samuel 20, outside this scope (wrong_scope).

content: According to 2 Samuel 13, after killing Amnon, where did Absalom flee and take refuge?
options: The land of the Philistines
The wilderness of En-gedi
The city of Ziklag
The land of Geshur
explanation: 2 Samuel 13:37-38 records that Absalom fled to Talmai, king of Geshur, his maternal grandfather, and stayed there for three years. 'The land of the Philistines' is where David took refuge from King Saul in 1 Samuel, not Absalom (wrong_scope). 'The wilderness of En-gedi' is also where David previously hid from Saul (wrong_scope). 'The city of Ziklag' is the city that Achish gave to David in 1 Samuel 27, outside this story (near_passage).

content: According to 2 Samuel 14, from which city did the wise woman come whom Joab sent to speak to David?
options: From Tekoa
From Abel
From Gibeon
From Bethel
explanation: 2 Samuel 14:2 records that Joab sent someone to Tekoa to bring a wise woman from there. 'Abel' is the city where another wise woman appears in 2 Samuel 20 — easy to confuse but a different context (near_passage). 'Gibeon' is where the battle between Abner's forces and Joab's forces took place in chapter 2, outside this story (wrong_scope). 'Bethel' is a well-known place of worship but has no connection to this passage (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Samuel 13, what scheme did Jonadab devise to give Amnon an opportunity to be alone with Tamar?
options: Pretend to be sick and ask his father to send Tamar to cook for him
Invite Tamar to the sheep-shearing feast with the king's sons
Send someone to invite Tamar to Absalom's house for a meal
Ask David to give Tamar in marriage since the law permitted it
explanation: 2 Samuel 13:3-5: Jonadab told Amnon to lie down and pretend to be ill, and when the king came to visit, to ask that Tamar come and make bread before him for him to eat. 'Inviting her to the sheep-shearing feast' is confused with Absalom's later scheme to kill Amnon (near_passage). 'Inviting her to Absalom's house' gets the character and location wrong, since the event took place at Amnon's house (wrong_detail). 'Asking David to give Tamar in marriage' echoes Tamar's own plea to Amnon in verse 13 but was not Jonadab's scheme (true_but_off).

content: According to 2 Samuel 13, after sinning against Tamar, how did Amnon's attitude toward her change?
options: He asked David to let him marry her as his wife
He repented and sent her back to her father's house with honor
He hated her with a hatred even greater than the love he had felt for her
He kept her in his house as a concubine
explanation: 2 Samuel 13:15 records that Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her, and he drove her out. 'Asking to marry her' was what Tamar herself had pleaded for but Amnon refused — it was not something Amnon did (true_but_off). 'Repenting and sending her back with honor' completely reverses the text, which shows he humiliated and drove her away (wrong_detail). 'Keeping her as a concubine' contradicts verse 17, where he commanded his servant to put her out and bolt the door after her (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Samuel 14, what situation of the king did the story told by the woman of Tekoa cleverly mirror?
options: That David had once pardoned someone who cursed him
That David had allowed his son to live in exile for killing his brother
That David was surrounded by enemies with no way of escape
That David had lost his firstborn son with Bathsheba
explanation: 2 Samuel 14:5-11: She told of two sons, one of whom killed the other, and the family demanded the death of the surviving son; she had David swear to protect the living son's life — then applied it to the king's own situation, urging him to call back Absalom, who was in exile for having killed Amnon. 'Pardoning someone who cursed him' alludes to Shimei in chapter 16, outside the scope of this passage (near_passage). 'Being surrounded by enemies' was not the intent of the story, which concerns forgiving a son (wrong_detail). 'Losing his firstborn son with Bathsheba' is a real event in chapter 12 but is not what this parable refers to (true_but_off).

content: According to 2 Samuel 14, what was highlighted as a notable sign of Absalom's beauty?
options: His stature was taller than all the people
His face looked exactly like his father King David
His hair weighed two hundred shekels when cut each year
His complexion and eyes were as beautiful as David's when he was young
explanation: 2 Samuel 14:25-26 praises Absalom as having no blemish from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, and records that when he cut his hair at the end of every year — because it was heavy on him — it weighed two hundred shekels by the king's weight. 'Stature taller than all the people' is the description given to Saul in 1 Samuel 9, not Absalom (wrong_scope). 'His face looked like his father' is a detail not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'His complexion and eyes were beautiful' borrows the description of David at his anointing in 1 Samuel 16 and wrongly applies it to Absalom (near_passage).

content: According to 2 Samuel 13, comparing the reactions of those involved after Tamar was violated, which description is MOST accurate to the text?
options: Tamar remained silent and hid the matter, while Absalom immediately reported to the king demanding that Amnon be punished
Tamar tore her robe and went away weeping; Absalom told her to be quiet; and David was angry but did not punish Amnon
David immediately drove Amnon from his house, while Absalom comforted Tamar and brought her back to their father
Tamar ran to David for help, and the king angrily ordered Amnon to be seized at once
explanation: Combining the verses: 13:19 Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe that she wore, and she laid her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went; 13:20 Absalom said to her, 'Be quiet for now, my sister... Do not take this to heart'; 13:21 when King David heard all these things, he was very angry, but the text does not record that the king punished Amnon. Option A is wrong because Absalom did NOT report to the king — instead he told Tamar to be silent (wrong_detail, almost-right). Option C is wrong because David did not drive Amnon out, and it was Absalom himself who took Tamar into his own house — he did not bring her back to their father (wrong_detail, almost-right). Option D is wrong because David was angry but gave no order to seize Amnon (wrong_detail). The question requires precise identification of who did what among the three characters.

content: According to 2 Samuel 14, although permitted to return home, what drastic action did Absalom ultimately take in order to finally gain an audience with David?
options: He sent his servants to set fire to Joab's barley field to force Joab to come meet him
He stood at the city gate and pleaded with the people one by one to appeal on his behalf to the king
He himself came and knelt before the palace gate for many days waiting for the king to take notice of him
He offered sacrifices at Hebron and asked the priests to convey his request to the king
explanation: 2 Samuel 14:28-33: Absalom lived two years in Jerusalem without seeing the king's face; after Joab twice refused to come to him, Absalom sent his servants to set Joab's barley field on fire, which compelled Joab to come — and through Joab he was finally brought in to the king, who kissed him. Option B borrows Absalom's tactic of standing at the city gate to win the hearts of the people in chapter 15 — right character but wrong context and purpose (near_passage, almost-right). Option C describes a submissive, pleading posture not found in the text, which portrays Absalom as actively compelling a response (wrong_detail, almost-right). Option D confuses this with the sacrifice at Hebron that Absalom later used as a pretext for his rebellion — it was not how he gained an audience with the king (near_passage).

content: To which city did Absalom ask King David's permission to go, claiming he needed to fulfill a vow he had made while living in Geshur in Aram?
options: Hebron
Jerusalem
Giloh
Mahanaim
explanation: 2 Samuel 15:7-8 records that Absalom asked to go to Hebron to fulfill a vow he had made, and it was there that he conspired to have himself proclaimed king. Jerusalem is where David was reigning, not the city Absalom asked to go to (wrong_detail). Giloh was the hometown of Ahithophel, the counselor who defected to Absalom, not Absalom's stated destination (near_passage). Mahanaim is where David later fled during the rebellion, which falls outside the scope of this episode (wrong_scope).

content: Which of David's renowned counselors abandoned the king and defected to Absalom during the rebellion?
options: Joab
Ahithophel
Hushai
Abishai
explanation: 2 Samuel 15:12 states that Absalom sent for Ahithophel, David's counselor, from the city of Giloh to join him. Joab was David's commander-in-chief and remained loyal to the king (wrong_detail). Hushai, by contrast, was secretly sent by David to infiltrate Absalom's inner circle and undermine Ahithophel's counsel (common_misconception). Abishai was Joab's brother, a mighty warrior who stayed loyal to David (wrong_detail).

content: When David fled Jerusalem, what did the king instruct the priests to do with the ark of the covenant?
options: Carry the ark with the king to the battlefield
Carry the ark back into the city of Jerusalem
Hide the ark in a cave in the wilderness
Take the ark to the land of Gath for refuge
explanation: 2 Samuel 15:25 records that David told Zadok to carry the ark of God back into the city, trusting that if the LORD showed him favor, he would bring the king back to see it again. Taking the ark out to battle is precisely what David deliberately refused to do (wrong_detail). Hiding the ark in a cave is not found anywhere in the text (wrong_detail). Taking the ark to Gath confuses this with the Gittites who followed the king — it was those people, not the ark, who accompanied David from Gath (near_passage).

content: When David had passed the summit of the Mount of Olives, who came to meet him with a pair of donkeys loaded with bread, raisins, and wine?
options: Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth
Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan
Barzillai the Gileadite
Ittai the Gittite
explanation: 2 Samuel 16:1 records that Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, met David with two donkeys loaded with bread, raisins, and wine. Mephibosheth was Ziba's master, and Ziba falsely accused him of remaining in Jerusalem to reclaim his grandfather's throne (common_misconception). Barzillai the Gileadite did supply David with provisions, but at Mahanaim — a separate episode outside the scope of this scene (wrong_scope). Ittai the Gittite was a military commander who followed the king into exile, not the one who brought provisions (near_passage).

content: How did Absalom gradually win the hearts of the people of Israel before his rebellion?
options: He stood beside the city gate, greeted those coming with lawsuits warmly, and lamented that no one had been appointed by the king to hear their cases
He distributed food and money to the poor every morning at the temple
He led troops to victory over neighboring nations so the people would praise his military prowess
He publicly accused corrupt judges and seated himself on the judgment throne in the palace
He promised to reduce taxes for all the tribes if they would make him king
explanation: 2 Samuel 15:2-6 describes Absalom rising early and standing along the road by the city gate, intercepting those who came to bring a dispute before the king, telling them there was no one appointed by the king to hear them, and wishing he were made judge — and so he 'stole the hearts of the men of Israel.' The option about distributing food at the temple is invented and has no basis in the text (wrong_detail). Defeating neighboring nations was David's military achievement, not the method Absalom employed (wrong_scope). Seating himself on the throne in the palace gets the location wrong: Absalom stood outside the city gate and never formally presided over any court proceedings (near_passage). Promising to reduce taxes sounds politically plausible but does not appear anywhere in the passage (common_misconception).

content: Why did David not allow Hushai the Archite to flee with him, but instead told him to return to Jerusalem?
options: To have Hushai remain as a false counselor for Absalom in order to thwart the counsel of Ahithophel
Because Hushai was too old and weak to keep pace with the king's fleeing company
To have Hushai watch over the ten concubines the king left behind to keep the palace
Because Hushai needed to stay and guard the ark of the covenant with the priests in the city
explanation: 2 Samuel 15:34 records that David told Hushai to return and tell Absalom he would serve the new king, so as to 'defeat the counsel of Ahithophel' on David's behalf. The reason of old age belongs to Barzillai later, not Hushai (near_passage). Watching over the ten concubines was something David left them to do themselves, not a task assigned to Hushai (wrong_detail). Guarding the ark of the covenant was the duty of Zadok and Abiathar, not Hushai (wrong_detail).

content: What did Ziba tell David about his master Mephibosheth, and what did the king decide to grant Ziba as a result?
options: That Mephibosheth had stayed behind hoping the house of Saul would be restored to the throne; the king gave all his master's property to Ziba
That Mephibosheth had joined Absalom's forces; the king ordered Mephibosheth to be arrested
That Mephibosheth was gravely ill and unable to travel; the king sent medicine to his master
That Mephibosheth had fled to another land; the king divided the property equally between the two
explanation: 2 Samuel 16:3–4 records that Ziba falsely claimed Mephibosheth had stayed in Jerusalem hoping Israel would restore his grandfather's kingdom to him; David then declared, 'All that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours.' The dividing of the property only happened later in chapter 19, not at this point (wrong_scope). Saying Mephibosheth led troops for Absalom is a fabricated detail — Ziba only said he stayed behind (wrong_detail). Sending medicine is not in the text, even though Mephibosheth was indeed lame (common_misconception).

content: When Abishai asked permission to cut off the head of the man cursing the king, how did David respond?
options: He restrained Abishai, saying perhaps the LORD had told the man to curse, and hoping God would repay him with blessing
He agreed at once and sent Abishai across the ridge to behead the blasphemer
He laughed at the man, saying he was only a dead dog not worth his concern
He ordered his troops to bind the man so that when the king returned he could be tried fairly
explanation: 2 Samuel 16:10–12 records David restraining Abishai, saying 'let him curse, for the LORD has said to him,' and hoping God would see his affliction and repay him with blessing. Agreeing to have the man killed is the opposite of the king's actual response (wrong_detail). The phrase 'dead dog' was Abishai's own description of Shimei, not David's attitude (near_passage). Ordering the man bound for a later trial is not in the text at this point (wrong_detail).

content: Ahithophel advised Absalom to publicly go in to the concubines his father had left behind — for what purpose, and how highly did the people regard this counsel?
options: So that all Israel would know Absalom had made himself odious to his father, strengthening the resolve of his followers; his words were regarded like the word of God
To disgrace the concubines who had been unfaithful, taking personal revenge for his clan; his words were only half-believed by the people
To fulfill Nathan's prophecy about the disaster in David's household; his words were strongly opposed by the elders
To test the loyalty of the concubines to the former king; his words were only partially heeded by Absalom
explanation: 2 Samuel 16:21 records Ahithophel advising Absalom to go in to his father's concubines so that 'all Israel will hear that you have made yourself odious to your father,' thereby strengthening the hands of his supporters; verse 23 states that Ahithophel's counsel in those days was regarded 'as if one consulted the word of God.' The option about disgracing unfaithful concubines invents the motive and misstates the level of regard (wrong_detail). The option about Nathan's word is correct that this fulfills the foretold disaster (2 Sam 12:11–12), but Ahithophel was not aiming to fulfill prophecy, and his counsel was respected rather than opposed (true_but_off). The option about testing loyalty reverses both the purpose and the influence of the counsel (wrong_detail). One must compare the political motive stated in verse 21 with the counselor's authority described in verse 23 to choose correctly.

content: When David urged Ittai the Gittite to turn back because he was a foreigner who had only recently arrived, how did Ittai respond?
options: He swore that wherever the king went, whether in life or in death, his servant would be there with the king
He asked to return to Gath with his own people, not wishing to be involved in the king's household affairs
He proposed staying in Jerusalem to gather intelligence and report back to David through the priests
He begged the king to let him lead the troops ahead to scatter Absalom's forces before they could assemble
explanation: 2 Samuel 15:21 records Ittai swearing: 'As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will your servant be.' The option of asking to return to Gath was actually David's suggestion to Ittai, not Ittai's reply — the roles of the dialogue are reversed (near_passage). The option of staying to gather intelligence was what Hushai, Zadok, and Abiathar did, not Ittai (wrong_scope). The option of asking to lead troops ahead sounds fitting for a seasoned warrior but is not in the text (true_but_off). One must distinguish David's words from Ittai's and compare the roles of the various figures to choose correctly.

content: During Absalom's rebellion, who proposed selecting twelve thousand men to pursue David that very night?
options: Ahithophel
Hushai
Joab
Abishai
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 17:1, Ahithophel said to Absalom: 'Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight.' B (Hushai) was the one who gave the opposing advice to save David, not this plan (wrong_detail). C (Joab) was David's commander and was not on Absalom's side (wrong_scope). D (Abishai) was likewise a commander on David's side (wrong_scope).

content: Absalom and the men of Israel ultimately chose to follow whose advice instead of Ahithophel's?
options: Hushai the Archite
Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth
Zadok the priest
Amasa son of Ithra
explanation: 2 Samuel 17:14 states: 'The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel,' for the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel. B (Ziba) was the servant connected to Mephibosheth and did not give this advice (wrong_scope). C (Zadok) was a priest who assisted David, not a counselor to Absalom (wrong_detail). D (Amasa) was the man Absalom appointed as commander, not the counselor chosen here (near_passage).

content: When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been followed, what did he do upon returning to his own city?
options: He hanged himself
He fled to the land of Geshur
He surrendered and joined David
He was killed by Joab with a spear
explanation: 2 Samuel 17:23 records that Ahithophel went home, set his house in order, and hanged himself, and was buried in the tomb of his father. B (fleeing to Geshur) was where Absalom had previously taken refuge, not Ahithophel (near_passage). C (surrendering to David) contradicts the text (wrong_detail). D confuses this event with how Joab killed Absalom with spears in chapter 18 (wrong_scope).

content: During the battle, what did Absalom's head become caught in, leaving him hanging between heaven and earth?
options: The branches of a great oak tree
A protruding rock by the river
A net trap set by David's soldiers
The reins of his war horse
explanation: 2 Samuel 18:9 recounts that as Absalom was riding his mule under the thick branches of a great oak, his head caught fast in the oak and he was left hanging between heaven and earth while the mule went on. B (a rock) does not appear in the text (wrong_detail). C (a net trap) is a fabricated detail (common_misconception).
