D (the reins) is incorrect because it was the oak branches that caught his head, not the reins of his mule (wrong_detail).

content: How were the two messengers Jonathan and Ahimaaz hidden from Absalom's men at Bahurim?
options: A woman hid them in a well and spread grain over its opening to conceal it
A woman hid them on her rooftop under a pile of barley
They hid in a cave whose entrance was blocked with a large stone
They disguised themselves as shepherds and blended into a flock
explanation: 2 Samuel 17:18-19 records that the two men went down into a well at Bahurim, and the woman spread a covering over the well's mouth and scattered grain on it so no one knew they were there. B is close but confuses 'rooftop with barley' — echoing Rahab's concealment of the spies — with a well (common_misconception). C (a cave blocked by a stone) is entirely incorrect (wrong_detail). D (disguising as shepherds) does not appear in the text (wrong_detail).

content: Why did certain men at Mahanaim — Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai — bring beds, grain, flour, and food to David?
options: Because they believed the people were hungry and weary in the wilderness
Because David had ordered a requisition of food supplies for the army
Because they wanted to bribe their way to pardon for having sided with Absalom
Because the priest Zadok commanded them to bring the tithe to the king
explanation: 2 Samuel 17:29 states the reason: 'for they said, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness"' — so these men brought provisions voluntarily. B is wrong because this was a voluntary gift, not a forced requisition (wrong_detail). C reverses the motive: these men were loyal to David, not followers of Absalom (common_misconception). D — a tithe commanded by Zadok — is a fabricated detail with no basis in the text (wrong_scope).

content: Before sending the troops into battle, what does the special order David gave to Joab, Abishai, and Ittai reveal about his heart?
options: He still had compassion for Absalom, commanding them to deal gently with the young man
He was determined to punish the rebellion harshly in order to deter future revolts
He wanted to capture Absalom alive for a public trial before the people
He was more concerned for Joab and instructed the commanders to protect Joab above all
explanation: 2 Samuel 18:5 records David charging his commanders: 'Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom,' and all the people heard the king's charge — revealing a father's tender compassion. B directly contradicts the command to deal gently (wrong_detail). C comes close in that David wanted Absalom kept alive, but the purpose of 'a public trial' does not appear in the text (near_passage). D misidentifies who the king was concerned about in this verse (wrong_detail).

content: When Joab learned that Absalom was still alive, hanging in a tree, and that the soldier who found him had not dared to act, what did Joab do?
options: He took three javelins and thrust them into Absalom's heart, then let his armor-bearers strike him down
He personally hanged Absalom even higher on a branch of a nearby tree
He ordered soldiers to shoot arrows continuously until Absalom had fully stopped breathing
He ordered Absalom to be brought down from the tree and escorted back to King David for judgment
explanation: 2 Samuel 18:14-15 records that Joab took three javelins and thrust them into Absalom's heart while he was still alive in the tree, and then ten of Joab's armor-bearers surrounded Absalom and struck him dead. B is wrong — Absalom was caught by his head in the branches; Joab did not hang him (wrong_detail). C describes a different method of killing that does not match the text (wrong_detail). D contradicts Joab's deliberate act of killing despite the king's explicit command to deal gently (common_misconception).

content: Although Ahimaaz pleaded to carry the news of victory, Joab sent Cushi first. What does this division of roles reveal about Joab's intent?
options: Joab wanted to spare Ahimaaz from having to report the prince's death to the king
Joab believed Ahimaaz was a slower runner and would not arrive in time
Joab suspected Ahimaaz was loyal to Absalom and therefore would not send him
Joab kept Ahimaaz back to guard Absalom's body in the pit
explanation: 2 Samuel 18:19-22 shows Joab telling Ahimaaz, 'You shall not carry news today, for the king's son is dead,' before finally allowing him to run after Cushi — indicating Joab wished to shield Ahimaaz from delivering the grim report. B is wrong because Ahimaaz later outran Cushi and arrived first (18:23), so slowness was not the reason (near_passage). C reverses the facts: Ahimaaz was the son of Zadok and was loyal to David, not to Absalom (common_misconception). D confuses Ahimaaz's role with the act of throwing Absalom's body into the pit and piling stones over it, which was carried out by Joab's troops, not assigned to Ahimaaz (wrong_scope).

content: Comparing the two messengers, why did David still anxiously ask 'Is it well with the young man Absalom?' even after hearing news of victory from Ahimaaz?
options: Because Ahimaaz spoke evasively, and only Cushi, arriving afterward, disclosed Absalom's fate
Because Ahimaaz had confirmed that Absalom was dead and the king wanted to hear it again
Because both messengers reported that Absalom had escaped safely
Because Cushi arrived first with the victory report but withheld the news about Absalom
explanation: 2 Samuel 18:29 shows that when the king asked, Ahimaaz answered evasively: 'I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was.' Only when Cushi arrived (18:31-32) and said, 'May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you for evil be like that young man,' did David understand that Absalom was dead. B is wrong because Ahimaaz deliberately withheld the news of the death (near_passage). C contradicts the text — neither messenger reported that Absalom had escaped (wrong_detail). D reverses the sequence: Ahimaaz arrived first, Cushi arrived afterward (wrong_detail).

content: When David heard that his son had been killed in battle, he covered his face and cried out loudly, calling whose name?
options: Absalom
Amnon
Jonathan
Solomon
explanation: 2 Samuel 19:4: 'The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!' Amnon was the son killed by Absalom earlier, so this is not the occasion for mourning him (wrong_detail). Jonathan was David's friend who died in chapter 1, a different context (wrong_scope). Solomon was the son still alive who would later take the throne (wrong_scope).

content: Who rebuked David for mourning and causing his servants shame, and urged the king to go out and speak encouragingly to them?
options: Joab
Abishai
Shimei
Ahithophel
explanation: 2 Samuel 19:5-7: Joab went into the house to the king, rebuked him, and told the king to go out and speak encouragingly to his servants. Abishai was Joab's brother, who only demanded that Shimei be put to death and did not rebuke the king here (near_passage). Shimei was the one who had cursed David, not the one who counseled the king (wrong_detail). Ahithophel was Absalom's counselor and had already died before this point (wrong_scope).

content: When David returned after Absalom's defeat, a Benjaminite who had previously cursed the king hurried down to meet him and begged the king not to hold his sin against him. Who was this person?
options: Shimei
Sheba
Mephibosheth
Barzillai
explanation: 2 Samuel 19:16-20: Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet the king and confessed the sin of cursing him. Sheba was also a Benjaminite but was the one who rebelled against David afterward and never sought forgiveness (near_passage). Mephibosheth was Jonathan's son who came to meet the king, but out of loyalty — he had never cursed David (wrong_detail). Barzillai was the Gileadite who had provided for the king and had never cursed him (wrong_scope).

content: Why did Mephibosheth, the grandson of King Saul, neither trim his beard nor wash his clothes during the entire time David was fleeing?
options: To show his grief and mourning until the king returned safely
Because Ziba had abandoned him and left no one to care for him in the field
Because he had sided with Absalom and did not dare show his face
Because he was under a vow of abstinence before God
explanation: 2 Samuel 19:24: Mephibosheth 'had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety,' demonstrating his loyal grief. Being abandoned by Ziba was not the reason; it was Ziba himself who had slandered Mephibosheth and seized his property (common_misconception). He did not side with Absalom — it was Ziba who falsely accused him of hoping to be restored to the throne (wrong_detail). No vow of abstinence is mentioned anywhere in this passage (wrong_scope).

content: The elderly Gileadite who had supplied David at Mahanaim declined the king's invitation to come to Jerusalem and live with him. What reason did he give?
options: He was eighty years old and could no longer tell good from bad or hear the voices of singers
He still had to remain in his hometown to look after his property and large herds
He feared the people of Jerusalem would be jealous of him because he was an outsider
He wanted to yield the honor of serving beside the king to his own descendants
explanation: 2 Samuel 19:34-35: Barzillai answered that he was already eighty years old, could no longer discern good from bad, could not taste what he ate or drank, and could not hear the voices of men and women singing — so he did not want to be a burden to the king. The reason of overseeing his property is never mentioned (wrong_detail). The fear of being envied is speculation not found in the text (wrong_scope). He did ask the king to show kindness to Chimham in his place, but his stated reason for declining was old age, not 'yielding the honor to his descendants' (true_but_off).

content: At the end of chapter 19, the men of Israel and the men of Judah argued bitterly about bringing the king back across the Jordan River. What was the core of the dispute between the two sides?
options: The men of Israel claimed they had ten shares in the king and accused Judah of secretly bringing the king across the river
The men of Judah demanded that the king establish his capital at Hebron rather than Jerusalem
The men of Israel wanted to make Sheba king instead of David
The men of Judah accused the men of Israel of having sided with Absalom against the king
explanation: 2 Samuel 19:41-43: The men of Israel rebuked Judah for secretly bringing the king and his household across the Jordan, while they claimed 'we have ten shares in the king' and therefore deserved a greater part; yet Judah's reply was harsher. The question of establishing the capital at Hebron is not the subject of the dispute here (wrong_scope). The revolt of Sheba belongs to chapter 20 and is a rebellion, not a debate about escorting the king back (near_passage). The accusation of siding with Absalom is not the argument raised in this particular dispute (wrong_detail).

content: Which Benjaminite blew the trumpet to incite rebellion, calling on the men of Israel to abandon David with the cry 'We have no share in David'?
options: Sheba son of Bichri
Shimei son of Gera
Abishai son of Zeruiah
Amasa son of Jether
explanation: 2 Samuel 20:1: 'There happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite' who blew the trumpet and called the men of Israel to abandon David. Shimei son of Gera was also a Benjaminite, but he was the man who had cursed David and then pleaded for mercy in chapter 19 — he did not lead a revolt (near_passage). Abishai was a loyal commander of David, not a rebel (wrong_detail). Amasa was the commander David sent to suppress the revolt, not its instigator (wrong_scope).

content: When David returned to his palace in Jerusalem, how did he treat the ten concubines who had been violated by Absalom?
options: He provided for them but confined them separately, never going in to them again; they lived as widows until they died
He expelled all of them from the palace and sent them back to their parents' homes
He ordered his soldiers to kill them all, considering them to have brought disgrace upon his honor
He elevated all of them to the rank of queen to make amends for the violation they had suffered
explanation: 2 Samuel 20:3: David provided food for the ten concubines but confined them, never going in to them; they were shut up until the day of their death, living as widows. The king did not send them back to their parents' homes (wrong_detail). The king did not kill them (common_misconception). Elevating them to the rank of queen flatly contradicts the text, since they were kept in confinement (wrong_scope).

content: At Gibeon, Joab pretended to greet Amasa warmly and then suddenly killed him. How is that treacherous act specifically described?
options: Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him, then stabbed him in the stomach so that his entrails poured out
Joab invited Amasa to a banquet and then signaled soldiers lying in ambush to stab him to death
Joab challenged Amasa to single combat and then cut him down with a dagger
Joab embraced Amasa from behind and strangled him to death
explanation: 2 Samuel 20:9-10: Joab said, 'Is it well with you, my brother?' then 'took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.' Amasa did not notice the sword in Joab's other hand, so Joab stabbed him in the stomach and his entrails poured out to the ground — he died with a single blow. There is no detail about inviting him to a banquet or soldiers lying in ambush (wrong_detail). There was no single combat with a dagger (wrong_scope). The method of killing was a sword thrust, not strangulation (common_misconception).

content: How did the siege of Sheba at the city of Abel Beth-maacah come to an end?
options: A wise woman negotiated with Joab, and the people of the city cut off Sheba's head and threw it over the wall
Joab built a siege ramp, broke down the wall of Abel, then stormed in and captured Sheba alive
Sheba slipped out of the city at night but was pursued and killed in the open field by David's troops
The people inside the city flung open the gates and handed Sheba over alive to Joab to be taken back for trial
explanation: 2 Samuel 20:16-22: A wise woman in the city negotiated with Joab; at her urging, the people cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it over the wall to Joab, so he withdrew his forces. The city wall was not broken down — the siege ramp had only just begun to be built when the woman intervened (near_passage). Sheba did not escape and get killed in the open field; he died inside the city (wrong_detail). Sheba was killed, not handed over alive to be put on trial (wrong_scope).

content: During David's reign, Israel suffered a disaster that lasted three consecutive years. What was this disaster?
options: Famine
Plague
Foreign invasion
Earthquake
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 21:1, 'There was a famine in the days of David for three years.' The correct answer is famine. 'Plague' (wrong_detail) was the disaster in chapter 24 after David took a census, not here. 'Foreign invasion' (wrong_scope) belongs to other battle chapters, not this particular disaster. 'Earthquake' (common_misconception) is not mentioned in this context.

content: When David inquired of the LORD about the cause of the famine, the LORD revealed that the sin was connected to the household of which former king?
options: Saul
Abner
Ish-bosheth
Nahash
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 21:1, the LORD said, 'There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death.' The correct answer is Saul. 'Abner' (near_passage) was Saul's commander but not a king. 'Ish-bosheth' (wrong_detail) was Saul's son who briefly reigned, but he was not the one who committed this sin. 'Nahash' (wrong_scope) was the king of the Ammonites in a different context.

content: Which people had Saul sought to destroy, even though Israel had previously sworn to spare them, thereby bringing bloodguilt upon the land?
options: The Gibeonites
The Philistines
The Amalekites
The Moabites
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 21:2, the Gibeonites were a remnant of the Amorites, and the people of Israel had sworn to spare them, but Saul had sought to kill them. The correct answer is the Gibeonites. 'The Philistines' (wrong_scope) are a different enemy who appear later in chapter 21 but have no connection to this oath of safe passage. 'The Amalekites' (common_misconception) were the people Saul was commanded to destroy in 1 Samuel 15, not here. 'The Moabites' (wrong_detail) have no involvement in this event.

content: To atone for the bloodguilt of Saul's house, the Gibeonites demanded that David hand over certain descendants of Saul. How did David fulfill their demand?
options: He handed over seven of Saul's descendants to be hanged before the LORD
He paid the Gibeonites a great sum of silver and gold to redeem the bloodguilt
He exiled all the remaining descendants of Saul's household from Israel forever
He offered a burnt offering of many cattle and sheep at the town of Gibeon
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 21:8-9, David handed over seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites, and they were hanged on the mountain before the LORD. The correct answer is that he handed over seven men to be hanged. 'Paying silver and gold' (common_misconception) is wrong because the Gibeonites themselves explicitly said, 'It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul' (v. 4) — they demanded lives. 'Exiling the descendants from the land' (wrong_detail) did not happen; they were executed, not banished. 'Offering cattle and sheep as a sacrifice' (wrong_scope) is a different form of atonement not used here. Distractors: wrong silver-gold payment (common_misconception), wrong exile (wrong_detail), wrong sacrificial offering (wrong_scope).

content: Rizpah, Saul's concubine, performed a moving act to protect the bodies of those who were hanged. What did she do?
options: She spread sackcloth on a rock and kept watch, preventing birds of the air and beasts of the field from coming near
She secretly buried the bodies at night in her family tomb
She went and pleaded with King David to allow her to take down the bodies for burial
She brought fragrant oil and burial cloths to the place to anoint the bodies of her sons
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 21:10, Rizpah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell on them from the sky, and she did not allow the birds of the air to come upon them by day, or the beasts of the field by night. The correct answer is that she spread sackcloth and kept watch. 'Secretly burying them at night' (wrong_detail) is wrong because she guarded the bodies in place; the formal burial was later carried out by David himself (vv. 13–14). 'Pleading with David to take them down' (near_passage) was not her action; it was David who, upon hearing what she had done, went and collected the bones. 'Bringing fragrant oil to anoint the bodies' (common_misconception) is not mentioned in this context. Distractors: wrong secret burial (wrong_detail), wrong role of petitioning the king (near_passage), wrong anointing (common_misconception).

content: Moved by Rizpah's actions, David arranged for the decent burial of whose bones together with those of the men who had been hanged?
options: The bones of Saul and Jonathan
The bones of Abner and Amasa
The bones of Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth
The bones of Samuel and Eli
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 21:12-14, David brought the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead and buried them together with the bones of those who had been hanged in the territory of Benjamin. The correct answer is Saul and Jonathan. 'Abner and Amasa' (wrong_scope) were commanders buried in different contexts. 'Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth' (wrong_detail) were sons/grandsons of Saul but not the bones brought back here. 'Samuel and Eli' (wrong_scope) are figures from 1 Samuel. Distractors: wrong commanders (wrong_scope), wrong descendants (wrong_detail), wrong book's characters (wrong_scope).

content: During a battle against the Philistines, David grew weary and was nearly killed by a giant named Ishbi-benob. What does the subsequent event reveal about David's role in battles thereafter?
options: Abishai rescued the king, and the soldiers swore that David would never go out to battle again lest the lamp of Israel be extinguished
David killed the giant with his own hand and continued to lead troops into battle as usual
Joab rescued the king, and David decided to hand full command of the army over to Solomon
Abishai rescued the king, but David insisted on personally going into battle in subsequent campaigns
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 21:16-17, Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David's aid and struck down the Philistine; then David's men swore that the king would never go out to battle with them again 'lest the lamp of Israel be extinguished.' The correct answer is that Abishai rescued the king and the oath kept the king from the battlefield. 'David killed the giant himself and continued going to battle' (wrong_detail) is wrong on both counts: it was Abishai who rescued him, and the king was prohibited from going out to battle. 'Joab rescued the king... handed command to Solomon' (wrong_detail) names the wrong rescuer (Joab instead of Abishai) and invents a consequence not mentioned here (Solomon). 'Abishai rescued but David insisted on going to battle anyway' (true_but_off) is correct about the rescuer but reverses the outcome of the oath. One must analyze both the rescuer and the consequence to answer correctly. Distractors: wrong person and outcome (wrong_detail), wrong rescuer (wrong_detail), reversed outcome (true_but_off).

content: On what occasion did David sing the long song in chapter 22?
options: When the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul
When he had just been anointed king over all Israel
When he brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem
When his son Absalom died in battle
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 22:1, David sang this song 'on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul.' The correct answer is when he was delivered from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. 'When he was anointed king' (wrong_detail) refers to an earlier event, not the occasion of this song. 'When he brought the ark of the covenant' (wrong_scope) belongs to chapter 6. 'When Absalom died' (common_misconception) belongs to chapters 18–19, which is associated with a very different lament.

content: In the song of chapter 22, David describes the LORD intervening to rescue him with dramatic imagery from nature. Which images does he use?
options: Thunder from heaven, arrows that scattered the enemy, and the channels of the sea laid bare before His breath
Great hailstones and a pillar of fire leading the people by night
A rainbow over the clouds and morning dew covering the valleys at dawn
An east wind parting the sea and a pillar of cloud shielding the people during the day
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 22:14-16, the LORD thundered from heaven, shot arrows and scattered the enemy, and the channels of the sea were laid bare and the foundations of the world were exposed at the blast of His nostrils. The correct answer is thunder, arrows, and the sea bed laid bare. 'Great hailstones and a pillar of fire leading the way' (common_misconception) blends imagery from the Exodus that does not appear in this song. 'A rainbow and morning dew' (wrong_detail) are gentle images inconsistent with the fierce tone of this passage. 'An east wind parting the sea and a pillar of cloud' (wrong_scope) also borrows from the Red Sea event rather than from David's words here. Distractors: wrong Exodus imagery (common_misconception), wrong tone (wrong_detail), wrong Red Sea context (wrong_scope).

content: The closing verse of the song in chapter 22 directs the gaze beyond David personally. What is the most prominent theological emphasis in this conclusion?
options: The LORD shows steadfast love to David and his offspring forever
The LORD promises that David will never face any enemy again
The LORD commits to giving David wealth and wisdom greater than all kings
The LORD swears that the temple will be built by David's own hands
explanation: According to 2 Samuel 22:51, 'Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever.' The theological emphasis is on covenant steadfast love extending to his offspring forever. 'He will never face any enemy again' (common_misconception) contradicts the logic of the song itself, which speaks of defeating enemies rather than promising their permanent absence. 'Wealth and wisdom greater than all kings' (true_but_off) is a promise given to Solomon (1 Kings 3), not the conclusion of this song. 'The LORD swears David will build the temple' (wrong_detail) contradicts chapter 7, where David himself was specifically prohibited from building the temple. One must distinguish the eternal dynastic covenant from other promises. Distractors: wrong logic of the song (common_misconception), misattributed promise to Solomon (true_but_off), contradicts the Davidic covenant (wrong_detail).

content: In the list of David's mighty men in 2 Samuel 23, what was the elite front-rank group called?
options: The Three mighty men
The Seven mighty men
The Twelve mighty men
The Two mighty men
explanation: 2 Samuel 23 distinguishes the leading group of 'the Three' (Josheb-basshebeth, Eleazar, Shammah) from the later group of 'the Thirty.' 'The Seven mighty men' (wrong_detail) is a fabricated number not found in the text. 'The Twelve mighty men' (wrong_detail) confuses this with the number of the twelve tribes, not this elite group. 'The Two mighty men' (wrong_detail) is one person short of the clearly named group of three.

content: Three mighty men risked their lives to break through the Philistine camp to bring back to David something he was longing for — what was it?
options: Water from the well at the gate of Bethlehem
Bread from the city of Hebron
Wine from the region of En-gedi
Honey from the forest of Ephraim
explanation: 2 Samuel 23:15-16 records that David longed for water from the well at the gate of Bethlehem, and the three mighty men broke through the Philistine camp to draw it and bring it to him. 'Bread from the city of Hebron' (wrong_detail) gets both the type of provision and the place name wrong. 'Wine from the region of En-gedi' (wrong_detail) confuses this with the place where David once fled from Saul. 'Honey from the forest of Ephraim' (near_passage) is a detail from a different battle in the book, not this event.

content: When the three mighty men brought back the water from the well at Bethlehem, what did David do with it, and for what reason?
options: Poured it out as an offering to the LORD, because he regarded it as the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives
Drank it all immediately to show his deep appreciation for the valor of the three mighty men
Divided the water equally among the three men to drink together in honor of their courage
Carefully stored the water in the tabernacle as a sacred memorial
explanation: 2 Samuel 23:16-17 records that David refused to drink but poured the water out as an offering to the LORD, saying that drinking it would be like drinking the blood of the men who risked their lives to get it. 'Drinking it to show his appreciation' (common_misconception) is the reaction one might naturally expect but is the opposite of what David actually did. 'Dividing the water for all three to drink together' (wrong_detail) adds an action not found in the text. 'Storing it in the tabernacle' (wrong_scope) assigns a liturgical role to the water that is never mentioned.

content: Among the heroic deeds of Benaiah son of Jehoiada recorded in 2 Samuel 23, what did he do in a pit on a snowy day?
options: Killed a lion
Captured a bear alive
Struck down a large serpent
Struck down a wild ox
explanation: 2 Samuel 23:20 records that Benaiah went down into a pit and killed a lion on a snowy day. 'Captured a bear alive' (wrong_detail) substitutes a different animal not mentioned here. 'Struck down a large serpent' (wrong_detail) invents an animal not named in the text. 'Struck down a wild ox' (wrong_detail) is also the wrong animal compared to the lion in the text.

content: When David ordered a census of the people, who opposed him but ultimately had to submit to the king's command?
options: Joab, the commander of the army
Gad, the king's seer
Abishai, Joab's brother
Nathan, the prophet
explanation: 2 Samuel 24:3-4 records that Joab urged the king not to take the census, but the king's word prevailed over him and he went to carry it out. 'Gad, the seer' (near_passage) only appears afterward to deliver the announcement of judgment, not as the one who opposed the king at the outset. 'Abishai' (wrong_detail) is a mighty warrior but had no part in this dispute. 'Nathan' (wrong_scope) is the prophet who rebuked David in the matter of Bathsheba, and is unrelated to the census order here.

content: After David repented of taking the census, what did God send the prophet Gad to give him?
options: A choice of one of three punishments
An unconditional word of forgiveness for his sin
A command to destroy the census records he had taken
A demand to pay a ransom for every person counted
explanation: 2 Samuel 24:12–13 records that Gad came and set before David three options for him to choose: seven years of famine, three months of fleeing before enemies, or three days of plague. 'An unconditional word of forgiveness' (common_misconception) contradicts the actual punishment that was presented. 'Destroy the census records' (wrong_detail) is an action God never commanded. 'Pay a ransom for every person counted' (near_passage) recalls the ransom law for census-taking in Exodus, not the content of Gad's message here.

content: Of the three punishments offered, which disaster ultimately fell upon the people of Israel?
options: Plague
Famine
War
Drought
explanation: 2 Samuel 24:15 records that the LORD sent a plague on Israel, causing seventy thousand people to die. 'Famine' (near_passage) was one of the options Gad presented but not what occurred. 'War' (near_passage) also appears among the three options (fleeing before enemies) but David did not choose it. 'Drought' (wrong_detail) was not even among the three options offered.

content: When the angel stretched out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, what did David's prayer reveal about how he viewed his responsibility for the sin?
options: He acknowledged that he himself had sinned and asked that the calamity fall on him and his father's house, not harm the flock
He shifted all the blame onto General Joab for being the one who carried out the wrongful census order
He asked God to divide the punishment equally between the king and all the people since both shared the guilt
He pleaded for God to graciously forgive the people because they were the ones who had incited him to take the census
explanation: 2 Samuel 24:17 records David saying: 'Behold, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house.' He bore full responsibility without shifting it to anyone else. 'Shifting blame to Joab' (common_misconception) directly contradicts the king's own confession of guilt, even though Joab was indeed the one who carried out the order. 'Asking God to divide the punishment equally between the king and all the people' (true_but_off) sounds fair but is the opposite of David's deliberate act of bearing the punishment on behalf of the people. 'The people incited him' (wrong_detail) fabricates a detail not present in the text and contradicts his description of them as innocent sheep.

content: According to the prophet Gad, where was David to build an altar to the LORD?
options: The threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite
On Mount Moriah near the ancient city of Zion
The cave of Adullam in the wilderness
At the old altar in Gibeon
explanation: 2 Samuel 24:18 records that Gad told David to go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. 'Mount Moriah near Zion' (true_but_off) would later be associated with the Temple but is not the specific site Gad designated here. 'The cave of Adullam' (wrong_scope) was where David took refuge while fleeing Saul and has no connection to this altar. 'The old altar at Gibeon' (wrong_detail) was a different place of worship, not the site Gad commanded for this altar.

content: Araunah offered to give David the threshing floor along with oxen and wooden equipment for sacrifice at no cost; what principle of giving did David's response reveal?
options: He insisted on paying the full price, because he would not offer to the LORD a sacrifice that cost him nothing
He accepted the gift but promised to repay Araunah many times over at a later date
He refused both the threshing floor and the oxen and went to find a cheaper site to build the altar
He accepted only the oxen for the sacrifice but left the threshing floor with Araunah
explanation: 2 Samuel 24:24 records David saying he would not offer to the LORD his God burnt offerings that cost him nothing, then he paid fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and the oxen. 'Accepting the gift but promising to repay later' (true_but_off) sounds reasonable at first but is the opposite of David's principle of paying on the spot. 'Refusing both the floor and the oxen to find a cheaper place' (common_misconception) misunderstands the king's motivation — it was not frugality but willingness to bear the cost. 'Accepting only the oxen while leaving the floor with Araunah' (wrong_detail) contradicts the text, since David bought both the threshing floor and the oxen with his own silver.
